Is Super Micro Computer (SMCI) Fully Valued After Its New CFO Appointment?

SMCI
Trade SMCI on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Super Micro Computer (SMCI) is back in focus after the board appointed veteran finance executive Mark Long as Chief Financial Officer and Senior Vice President on 15 October 2026, replacing David Weigand.

Super Micro Computer's share price has swung sharply in recent weeks, falling 20.9% over the last 7 days and 19.1% over 30 days, even though the 90-day share price return is up 24.0% and the 5-year total shareholder return is roughly 8x. This suggests long-term holders have still seen substantial gains, while short-term momentum is fading as the market digests the fresh CFO appointment, new AI infrastructure product launches, and a mixed backdrop of strong order intake alongside legal and execution risks.

Compare how Super Micro Computer stacks up against other AI infrastructure plays by reviewing the hand picked 55 AI infrastructure stocks that are also reacting to this kind of news flow.

Super Micro Computer has the products, orders and leadership to appear positioned as a powerhouse again after this pullback. The real test now is whether that strength is already fully reflected in today's valuation.

Most Popular Narrative: 29% Overvalued

Super Micro Computer closed at $31.63, while the most followed narrative fair value sits at $24.50, which frames the stock as richly priced against that lens.

The risk of SMCI being drawn into the Department of Justice investigation appears high. A realistic concern is that the individuals accused of illegal sales to China could seek reduced penalties by cooperating with prosecutors and providing testimony against the company.

See why 48 investors see Super Micro Computer as 29% overvalued.

Result: Fair Value of $24.50 (OVERVALUED)

Still, two pressure points could upend that overvaluation story: a deeper Department of Justice drag on Super Micro Computer and any pullback from its largest customer.

Find out about the key risks to this Super Micro Computer narrative.

Another View On Super Micro Computer's Valuation

There is a very different read on Super Micro Computer when you look at simple market ratios. The stock trades on a P/E of 9.5x, while peers average 57.4x and the fair ratio is 41.9x. This points to a wide valuation gap that could either close or stay open for a long time.

That kind of disconnect can reflect real risk around legal and customer concentration issues, or it can reflect investors overreacting to event risk. The key question for you is which side of that story you believe is driving the current price, and how patient you are willing to be if the market takes time to decide.

title: Super Micro (SMCI) Won Over $60 Billion in Orders, Is the Discount Deserved?
detail:
Super Micro (SMCI) Won Over $60 Billion in Orders, Is the Discount Deserved?
Insider Monkey Team

SMCI
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Super Micro Computer (NASDAQ:SMCI) has spent October fielding questions about a smuggling case. A contractor linked to the company pleaded guilty earlier this month to helping ship servers loaded with advanced Nvidia chips to China, Reuters reported. Prosecutors say the scheme involved billions of dollars of U.S. AI technology. The company says it wasn't named as a defendant and that the case hasn't affected its business operations. If you're looking for more undervalued stocks to play AI, check out our report on the 10 Undervalued AI Stocks to Buy Now.

But the business keeps getting bigger, and the stock is priced as if it won't. Its multiple of expected earnings sits far below the sector's. The question is whether that discount fairly reflects the legal risk, or whether it undervalues a company whose sales keep climbing. On the facts so far, the second reading looks closer, with one big condition attached.

The company builds the server racks that run AI data centers, including liquid-cooled systems for Nvidia's newest chips. Its customers range from cloud providers to ordinary businesses. Its pitch is pre-assembled building blocks that get a data center running faster than buying parts one by one.

Vertiv vs. Eaton: Which AI Power Stock Offers More Cash Flow for the Price?
Orders Point to a Much Bigger Year

Sales for the fiscal year that ended in June reached $39.1 billion, up from $22.0 billion a year earlier. CEO Charles Liang said the company took in more than $60 billion of new orders over the year and added several hundred enterprise customers. It also entered the new year with a record backlog. Management is guiding to $65.0 billion to $72.0 billion in sales for fiscal 2027, a range whose low end sits well above all of last year. If you're interested in AI infrastructure, we recently compiled a report on 10 Fastest-Growing AI Infrastructure Stocks to Buy.

This kind of growth has a long record behind it. Over the past five years, sales have grown about 61.5% a year, so the latest jump extends a long run instead of starting one.

Profit Is Finally Catching Up

Growth has come with thin margins, and that is where the surprise sits. Gross margin for the full year was 10.8%. Then, in the June quarter, it jumped to 17.5%, and net income for the quarter reached $1,178 million, well above the year-earlier quarter.

A single quarter can't prove a new level. Over the past 12 months, operating margin was only 7.09%, so most of the year still looked like a low-margin business. If the June quarter holds, though, the company will earn far more on each dollar of sales than the full-year figure suggests.

Until now, someone in Taiwan who shipped a rack of AI servers to a buyer in China faced no direct criminal penalty at home. On October 16, 2026, Taiwan's Minister of Economic Affairs Kung Ming-hsin confirmed that Taipei plans to add AI servers and cutting-edge semiconductors to its controlled goods list. That would make these shipments a crime under the Foreign Trade Act.

Ivan Marc / Shutterstock.com

"About to" means the plan has been announced but is still waiting on the law. It needs a legal amendment, and Kung gave no timeline.

For shareholders of NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA), Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (NYSE:TSM) and Super Micro Computer (NASDAQ:SMCI), the effect is mixed. Closing the Taiwan channel could remove gray-market demand that never showed up in official China sales, but it also reduces regulatory risk around all three companies.

Friday's moves came with a broader chip selloff and had little to do with this news. NVIDIA closed at $214.13, down 1.43%, worth $5.17 trillion. title: Was The Run In Super Micro Stock Hiding In Plain Sight?
detail:
Was The Run In Super Micro Stock Hiding In Plain Sight?
Trefis Team
Fri, October 16, 2026 at 8:20 PM CDT 4 min read
SMCI
^GSPC
DELL
HPE
ANET
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Image from Pixabay

Shares of Super Micro Computer (SMCI) rose 45.1% between July 17 and October 15, 2026. The S&P 500 gained 4.1% over the same period. During this window, the company reported a record order backlog and set a fiscal 2027 revenue target of $65 billion to $72 billion. That figure sits well above its fiscal 2026 sales. If investors could read this demand in advance, early signs would point to a company lacking capacity rather than customers. The evidence would also highlight a business securing the funds needed to catch up. So what was Super Micro saying about its demand before July 17?

Super Micro Said Capital Held Back Production

Executives provided an answer nearly a year before this window opened. During the fiscal Q4 2025 call held August 5, 2025, they detailed a capital constraint that limited how quickly Super Micro could scale production. A complaint of this nature comes from a company with more demand than it can fund, not less.

Financial filings took time to reflect this demand. Revenue in fiscal Q1 2026, the quarter ended September 2025, fell 15.5% from a year earlier. The picture shifted in the quarter ended December, filed February 6, 2026, when revenue rose 123.4%. The quarter ended March, filed May 11, showed a 122.7% rise on the same basis. By May, the demand management had described earlier was appearing in Super Micro's sales.

In June, Super Micro Raised Money For AI Orders

The financial strategy became public five weeks before the July window opened. On June 9, 2026, Super Micro announced it would raise $7.0 billion in stock and stock-linked securities. The company said these funds would buy components for AI orders received in recent weeks for its advanced AI servers.

Fulfilling these new orders required billions of dollars in parts. Investors acting on the June 9 release paid less, not more. Shares closed 28% lower on June 10, the next session. A buyer that day was up about 20% by October 15. The evidence was readable in advance, but acting on it required buying a stock that had just fallen.

How Big Were Super Micro's New Orders?

Management reported on August 11 that Super Micro took in over $60 billion of new orders in fiscal Q4 2026, the quarter ended June. This total amounts to more than one and a half times the $39.1 billion the company sold in all of fiscal 2026. Peers also rallied over the window. Hewlett Packard Enterprise was up 38.1%, Dell Technologies gained 28.4%, and Arista Networks climbed 15.9%. Part of the gain was shared across the group, yet Super Micro rose more than all three.

Key Stats for Super Micro Stock

Current Price: $35.09

Target Price (Mid): ~$72

Street Target: ~$42

Potential Total Return: ~105%

Annualized IRR: ~16% / year

What Happened?

Super Micro Computer (SMCI) earned $2.23 billion of GAAP net income in fiscal 2026 (ended June 30). It still burned $6.97 billion of free cash flow on $39.06 billion of revenue.

That gap now belongs to Mark Long, Western Digital's (WDC) CFO from 2016 to 2019. The board appointed him effective October 14 to replace David Weigand, according to an SEC filing. The hire comes nearly two years after Super Micro committed to finding a more experienced finance chief. Its investor relations materials show revenue grew 77.8% in the same year the cash drained.

Why a Profitable Company Burned Nearly $7 Billion

Almost all of the burn came in one quarter. Free cash flow was negative $6.70 billion in the March quarter, then swung to positive $719 million in June.

Even so, June's operating cash flow of $747 million landed 83% below the Street's estimate. Consensus still sees fiscal 2027 free cash flow of around negative $1.3 billion. In June, Super Micro announced a $7 billion equity financing package that included an at-the-market stock program of up to $2 billion.

At the Goldman Sachs Communacopia + Technology Conference on September 10, Michael Staiger, SVP of Corporate Development, said capital intensity has been high and that Super Micro is working on customer terms and delivery timing. "So we're making conscious efforts to improve that as we move forward so that we can become self-funded downstream," he said. He added that returning capital to shareholders is "probably going to be a little while."

CEO Charles Liang said he is "confident Mark will have an immediate positive impact in strengthening and accelerating our operational and financial execution." Cash conversion is the most measurable place for that impact to show up.

Super Micro Free Cash Flows & Cash From Operations (TIKR)
The Selloff Started Before the CFO News

The stock was already under pressure when the CFO news hit. Benzinga tied the October 14 decline to two things. One was the export-control case, in which a contractor pleaded guilty on October 8 to helping divert servers with Nvidia (NVDA) chips to China. The other was a broad tech selloff. Shares closed at $35.78 that day.

Co-founder Wally Liaw, charged in the same case, has pleaded not guilty. Super Micro itself is not a defendant. Server peers also fell October 14 after Barclays cut Dell Technologies (DELL) and Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) to Equal Weight, and Dell dropped 11.4%.

CFOs On the Move: Week ending Oct. 16

Trading disclosure

This story was originally published on CFO.com. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily CFO.com newsletter.

Mark Long | Super Micro Computer

Super Micro Computer appointed Mark Long as the AI server maker's new senior vice president and chief financial officer. Long's earlier roles include co-founder and partner of investment firm Prime Impact Capital, senior adviser of McKinsey & Company and CFO and chief strategy officer of Western Digital. Long succeeds David Weigand, who has been CFO since February 2021. In December 2024, Super Micro said it would search for a new CFO as part of recommendations from an independent special committee that reviewed its accounting practices. The committee was formed after EY abruptly resigned as Super Micro's auditor, saying it questioned whether the firm was "committed to integrity and ethical values." The final investigation findings noted there was no management misconduct, but there were "lapses" regarding rehiring former employees who previously resigned after a 2017 audit committee investigation. 

Jeff Schrader | Sierra Space

Jeff Schrader, CFO of Sierra Space, has left the spacecraft maker to pursue a new professional opportunity, according to Bloomberg reporting. Schrader joined the company in March as chief strategy officer from Lockheed Martin Space, and took over as Sierra Space's chief financial officer in June. Schrader started his career as a U.S. Air Force financial analyst, advancing to CFO for special programs and later the Air Force Rapid Capabilities Office. Schrader's departure brings questions about the timing of Sierra Space's long-awaited IPO, which the company has been discussing since 2024. 

Joseph Sesin | Denver Broncos

Joseph Sesin was named finance chief of the Denver Broncos. Sesin joins the NFL team from Angel City Football Club of the National Women's Soccer League, where he was most recently senior vice president of finance and accounting. Before that, he was senior vice president of accounting and finance for SoFi Stadium, YouTube Theater and Hollywood Park in Los Angeles. He started his career at J.P. Morgan, where he worked for over eight years, most recently as vice president. Sesin succeeds longtime CFO Justin Webster, who left in August. Webster joined the organization in 2010 and took over as chief financial officer in 2013. 

Anne Giviskos | MoonPay

Anne Giviskos was appointed finance chief of MoonPay, a global financial technology firm that provides payment and trading infrastructure for digital assets. Giviskos was most recently interim CFO and chief accounting officer at business travel and expense platform Navan. Earlier roles include chief risk and compliance officer at Euronext and director of finance at the New York Stock Exchange.
